title: Zapotec Civilization
capsule: The Zapotec civilization emerged in the Oaxaca Valley of southern Mexico around 500 BC with the founding of Monte Albán, one of Mesoamerica's earliest cities, which served as the political and ceremonial capital for over a millennium. At its peak during Monte Albán III (c. 200–700 AD), the polity controlled an estimated 2,000 settlements across the valley system and pioneered a syllabic writing system, a 260-day ritual calendar, and danzante bas-reliefs depicting sacrificed captives. Monte Albán was largely abandoned by 700–900 AD as regional power dispersed to successor city-states like Mitla and Yagul, possibly due to drought and competition from expanding Teotihuacan and later Mixtec polities. Zapotec-speaking communities retained significant political autonomy in parts of Oaxaca into the Spanish colonial era.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core territory around the Oaxaca Valley is archaeologically well-established; outer boundaries of political influence versus cultural spread are debated, and the geometric polygon likely approximates a maximum cultural extent rather than a precise administrative territory.
